FOR FAMILIES

You do not have to wait for everyone else to agree that something is wrong.

Your concern is enough reason to pause, look clearly at what is happening, and take seriously the way it affects you.

What happens to you along the way?

When a loved one’s drinking becomes unpredictable, your attention can narrow around them. You listen to their voice and footsteps, watch their mood, track money, and measure every promise. There may be less and less room to notice your own exhaustion, fear, and needs.

This is not weakness. It is a human response to ongoing uncertainty. The goal is not to label the other person. It is to understand your own reality more clearly.

Stay with what you can observe

“You are an alcoholic” can become an argument. “You came home unsteady last night, our child was scared, and I did not sleep” describes an event and its impact.

Support or rescue?

Support helps another person do what they are willing to take responsibility for. Rescue absorbs the consequences for them—covering, lying, paying, cleaning up, or arranging one more second chance.

A boundary is not a punishment

A boundary states what you will do to protect your time, safety, or well-being: “I will not ride with you if you have been drinking.” “I will discuss important issues only when you are sober.” “If you yell at me, I will leave the conversation.”

Clarity

Write down what happened without explaining it away.

Boundaries

Choose something based on your own actions that you can follow through on.

Safety

If violence, threats, or impaired driving are possible, get support before confronting the situation.
